questions.q: Classify each of the following as a scalar or a vector quantity: (i) 50 kg of rice, (ii) 20 m/s towards east, (iii) 100 J of energy, (iv) 30 N force acting downwards, (iv) 40°C temperature, (vi) 5 km displacement north-east.
questions.a: (i) Scalar (mass has only magnitude), (ii) Vector (velocity has magnitude and direction), (iii) Scalar (energy has only magnitude), (iv) Vector (force has magnitude and direction), (v) Scalar (temperature has only magnitude), (vi) Vector (displacement has magnitude and direction). A wrong answer like "20 m/s is scalar because it's speed" reveals confusion between speed (scalar) and velocity (vector). If a student says "force is scalar because it's measured in newtons", they are confusing unit with quantity type.

questions.q: Two vectors **a** and **b** are drawn in a plane. **a** starts at (1,2) and ends at (4,6). **b** starts at (-2,-1) and ends at (1,3). Are **a** and **b** equal? Justify your answer without calculating coordinates.
questions.a: Yes, **a** and **b** are equal. Both represent a displacement of 3 units right and 4 units up (magnitude 5, direction tan⁻¹(4/3)). Equality of vectors depends ONLY on magnitude and direction, not on initial/terminal points. A student who says "No, because they start at different points" has not grasped the free vector concept. A student who says "Yes, because both have magnitude 5" is incomplete — direction must also match.

questions.q: Draw a vector **v** of magnitude 6 cm making an angle of 30° with the positive x-axis. Then draw: (a) a unit vector in the direction of **v**, (b) the negative of **v**, (c) a vector collinear with **v** but twice its magnitude. Label magnitudes and directions clearly.
questions.a: (a) Unit vector: magnitude 1 cm, same direction (30°). (b) Negative: magnitude 6 cm, direction 210° (or 30°+180°). (c) Collinear vector: magnitude 12 cm, same direction 30° (or opposite if negative scalar). A student drawing the unit vector with magnitude 6 cm confuses "unit vector" with "vector of unit length in same direction" — they are the same, but the magnitude must be exactly 1. A student drawing the negative vector at 30° instead of 210° has not understood that negative reverses direction by 180°.

questions.q: Given three vectors: **p** = zero vector, **q** = unit vector along x-axis, **r** = vector of magnitude 5 at 60° to x-axis. Which of the following statements are ALWAYS true? (i) **p** is collinear with **q**. (ii) **q** and **r** are coinitial if drawn from origin. (iii) **p** + **q** = **q**. (iv) **q** and -**q** are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction.
questions.a: (i) True — zero vector is considered collinear with every vector (by convention, it has any direction). (ii) True — if both are drawn from origin, they share the same initial point. (iii) True — zero vector is additive identity. (iv) True — by definition of negative vector. A student marking (i) false doesn't know the convention that zero vector is parallel to all vectors. A student marking (ii) false thinks coinitial requires them to be drawn from the same point in a specific diagram, not that they CAN be drawn coinitial.

questions.q: A student writes: "Two vectors are equal if they have the same magnitude." Another student writes: "Two vectors are collinear if they have the same direction." Evaluate both statements and correct them.
questions.a: First statement is FALSE. Equal vectors require BOTH same magnitude AND same direction. Counterexample: 5 N east vs 5 N north — same magnitude, different directions, not equal. Second statement is FALSE. Collinear vectors are parallel to the same line — they can have same OR opposite directions. Example: 3i and -4i are collinear (both along x-axis) but directions are opposite. Corrections: "Two vectors are equal iff they have same magnitude AND same direction." "Two vectors are collinear iff they are parallel to the same line (i.e., one is a scalar multiple of the other)." A student who only corrects one part shows partial understanding of the definitions.

questions.q: Create a real-world scenario (Indian context) involving at least three different types of vectors from this node. Describe the scenario, identify each vector by type, and explain why it fits that type. Your scenario must include a zero vector naturally (not forced).
questions.a: Example: A delivery drone flies from a warehouse (point W) to a customer's house (point H) — displacement vector **d₁** (type: vector, magnitude 2 km, direction 30° north of east). It hovers at H for 5 minutes — displacement during hover is zero vector **0** (type: zero vector, magnitude 0, no definite direction). Then it flies to another house (point K) — displacement **d₂** (type: vector). The vectors **d₁** and **d₂** are coinitial if both drawn from W? No, they are not coinitial (different initial points). But the unit vector in direction of **d₁** is **û** = **d₁**/|**d₁**| (type: unit vector). A good answer identifies at least three types correctly with reasoning. A poor answer forces zero vector artificially (e.g., "a vector of magnitude 0") without a natural physical situation.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A vector is a quantity that possesses both magnitude (a non-negative real number ______ length or size) and direction (orientation in space).
Fill in the blank: Imagine a cricket bowler running up to ______ the ball.
Fill in the blank: The magnitude of a vector a is denoted by |a| or ‖a‖ and is always ≥ ______.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can: (1) Distinguish between scalar and vector quantities in real-world scenarios and give three examples of each with correct units.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ a cricket bowler running up to deliver the ball.
